full_judgment:
MM Ruhul Amin J : This appeal by leave is directed against the judgment and order dated 30-11-1998 passed by a Single Bench of the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 3961 of 1996 discharging the Rule. 

 2. Short facts are that the plaintiff-respondent filed Title Suit No.196 of 1977 in the 2nd Court of Munsif (now Assistant Judge), Gazipur Sadar for a decree for permanent injunction restraining the principal defendants from entering into the suit land and from planting any plant in the suit land and/or from in any way disturbing possession of the plaintiffs in the suit land stating, inter alia that on 4-5-1949 the Bhawal Court of Wards Estate settled the land in schedule 'A' to plaintiff Nos. 1-4 and proforma defendant No.6 on receipt of salami also settled lands of schedule 'B' to plaintiff Nos. 1 and 5 and proforma defendant Nos. 7-14 by realising salami from them and they were delivered possession of the suit land. The plaintiff Nos. 3-5 cultivated their own land and also cultivated and looked after the lands of others as bargaders. In a portion of schedule 'B' lands plaintiffs have erected huts where their caretaker Shamsuddin along with some cooks reside. During RS operation up to draft publication the suit land was recorded in the names of the plaintiffs and proforma defendants. Thereafter, the defendants filed objection under Rule 30 of Tenancy Rules and the objection officer ordered for recording the names of the defendants in place of the plaintiffs in the Khatian. On appeal the appellate officer directed for preparing the records in the names of the plaintiffs. The defendant then realised rent from the plaintiffs up to 1382 BS. The plaintiffs have been possessing the suit land uninterruptedly by cultivating seasonal crops. The principal defend ants have been threatening the plaintiffs to dispossess by growing Gazari trees on the suit land. Hence the suit. 

 4. The learned Munsif (now Assistant Judge) Gazipur Sadar) decreed the suit for permanent injunction by judgment dated 27-2-1982. Being aggrieved the defendants preferred Title Appeal No.147 of 1985 but the same was dismissed by the learned Subordinate Judge, (now Joint District Judge) Gazipur by judgment dated 11-1-1993. Being aggrieved the defendants preferred Civil Revision No. 3961 of 1996 and the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division discharged the Rule affirming the judgment of the appellate Court by judgment dated 30-11-1998. 

 5. Leave was granted to consider the submission that the plaintiffs having failed to prove their settlement and having at no stage challenged the notification under section 4 of the Forest Act cannot raise objection regarding non-publication of notification under section 20 of the said Act and also the submission that the High Court Division was wrong in not taking into consideration that the alleged settlements of the plaintiffs are simply unauthorised for want of approval by the Chief Manager of the Bhawal Court of Wards Estate and those are fictitious and therefore, the plaintiffs possession in part of the suit plots is not lawful and the plaintiffs being trespassers cannot get a decree for permanent injunction and the further submission that the High Court Division ought to have held that a simple suit for permanent injunction is not maintainable when complicated question of title is involved and the plaintiffs have failed to prove their lawful possession. 

 6. We have heard Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, the learned Additional Attorney-General for the appellants and Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, the learned Counsel for respondent Nos. 1,2 (a) to 2(g) & 3(a) to 3(c) and 4 and perused the judgment of the High Court Division and other connected papers. 

 7. It is not disputed that the suit plot Nos. 1662, 1600, 1596, 1606, 1350 and 1410 of mouza Araisha Proshad, District Dhaka (now Gazipur) were recorded in CS Khatian Nos. 158 and 81 as Gazari Garh and pond in the names of Zaminders of Bhawal Courts of Wards Estate. It is also not disputed that Notification No. 38 For dated 12th January, 1934 (Exhibit-A) was published in the Government Gazette by the Secretary of the then Government of Bengal declaring the suit plots and other plots in the District of Mymensingh and Dhaka as protected forest on terms which have been mutually agreed upon between the Board of Revenue and the Government of Bengal. It was further mentioned that the provisions of section 2, sections 29 to 34 (both inclusive), sections 41 and 42 and sections 76 to 78 (both inclusive) of the Forest Act, 1927, shall apply to the said lands which shall be managed as a protected forest. It is also not disputed that by another notification No.14177 For dated 17th July, 1937 (Exhibit-A-I) the schedule appended to the earlier notification No.38 For of 12-1-1934 (Exhibit-A) was substituted. In this notification also the suit plots were included. By another notification No.3125 For. dated 13th April, 1955 (Exhibit-A-2) published in the official Gazette, the Government decided to constitute a reserve forest with the lands comprised within the revisional survey plots described in the schedule of the notifications including the suit plots in the district of Dhaka. The Collector, Dhaka was appointed to act as Forest Settlement Officer to inquire into and examine the existence, nature and extent of any right alleged to exist in favour of any person in or over any land comprised within the boundaries specified in the schedule of the notification Exhibit-A(2). 

 The case of the plaintiffs is that, they took settlement of the suit plots from Bhawal Court of Wards Estate on 4-5-1949 on payment of salami and rent, etc by two salami receipts subject to the approval by the Chief Manager of the Estate. Photo copies of the salami receipts have been incorporated in the additional paper book filed by the appellant. From these salami receipts it appears that settlement was granted subject to approval by the Chief Manager of the Estate. But in the same receipt it was written on the same date that approval by the Chief Manager of the estate was duly accorded. This appears to be highly improbable. The plaintiffs also filed photo copies of Khatian No.B/412 of Mouza Araisha Proshad, PS Keraniganj, District-Dhaka to show that their names were duly mutated in the Khatian by order dated 16-10-1934 and on this date below the signature of the authorised officer the figure 34 is overwritten without any authentication. 

 9. It was borne out from the record that plaintiffs in this case examined three witnesses including plaintiff No.1 Abdur Rahman as PW 1 and PW 2 Abul Kashem (plaintiff No.3) and PW 3 Omizuddin who allegedly was borgader of the plaintiffs in the suit land. No witness was examined to prove the alleged settlement of the suit land in favour of the plaintiffs by Bhawal Court of Wards Estate. 

 13. It appears that the courts below did not at all consider the effect of Gazette notification dated 12th January, 1934 (Exhibit-A) treating the suit land as Protected Forest and the Gazette Notification dated 17th July, 1937 Exhibit-A(1) and 13th April, 1955 Exhibit-A(2), conveying the decision of the Government to constitute the suit land as reserved forest. This goes to show that since 1934 the suit lands were treated as forest land and the Government as back as in 1955 decided to constitute a reserved forest with the suit lands and other lands. 

 17. We also do not find any cogent reason to disbelieve Exhibit-B, an agreement made on 22nd June, 1954 between one Jnan Chandra Dhar and the Government for sale of Gazari trees from the suit plots and other plots. The learned Additional Attorney-General next argued that since a complicated question of title is involved in the matter, a simple suit for permanent injunction is not maintainable and the courts below lost sight of this important aspect of the matter. The learned Additional Attorney-General has cited the case of Abu Musa vs Bangladesh reported in 2 BLC (AD) 56 and submitted in that case, it was held that since the salami receipts were not proved by the Chief Manager of the Estate, the High Court Division has rightly found that no lease was granted in favour of the plaintiffs. In this case it was further held that as the plaintiffs failed to prove their settlement and did not challenge the notification under section 4 of the Act, it does not lie in their mouth to complain that there was no final notification under section 20 of the Act. The learned Additional Attorney-General further submitted that the facts of the cited case are similar to the facts of the case before us and the principles of law enunciated in that case are fully applicable in the present case. 

 19. Regarding maintainability of the suit, he submitted that the plaintiffs have already produced papers showing payment of rent and rent receipts are documents of possession. Therefore, a simple suit for permanent injunction at the instance of the plaintiffs who are in possession is maintainable. In support of his contention, he cited the case of Rafizuddin Ahmed vs Mongla Barman reported in 43 DLR (AD) 215. Mr Bhuiyan next argued that the provisions of section 6 of Forest Act having not been complied with, the question of extinction of right of the plaintiffs under section 9 of the Act does not arise. In reply, learned Additional Attorney- General submitted that since no objection was raised by plaintiffs regarding the Notifications Exhibits-A- A(2) issued by the Government treating the suit plots as forest lands since 1934, the provisions of section 6 shall be deemed to have been duly com- plied with and they cannot complain that there was no final notification under section 20 of the Act. He further submitted that since 1934 the property was treated as forest land, so Zaminder of Bhawal Court of Wards Estate had no authority to make any settlement of the suit land in the face of the above three notifications treating the suit lands firstly, as protected forest and then as reserved forest. 

 20. The plaintiffs could not prove their settlement and also could not show that the Bhawal Court of Wards Estate had authority to settle the suit land in the face of the notifications Exhibits-A-A(2). The courts below also did not take into consideration the broad fact that the salami receipts produced by the plaintiffs are private documents and these require strict proof for being admitted in evidence. 

 21. In view of the discussion above, we are of the view that the courts below committed error of law occasioning failure of justice in decreeing the plaintiffs' suit and this requires interference by this Court.
